paragraphs: Sparse training aims to reduce the resources needed to train large neural networks, but retaining good performance on unseen data remains difficult. This paper connects that difficulty to the structure of the training loss. The authors identify a chaotic loss surface associated with network sparsity, motivating an optimization method designed specifically for sparse networks.

Their method, S²-SAM, adapts sharpness-aware minimization into a single-step procedure. Its central move is to approximate the sharpness perturbation using gradient information already available from earlier updates. The authors report that this approximation adds no extra cost, allowing the method to pursue better generalization while preserving the efficiency motivation behind sparse training.

The paper studies generalization and provides a convergence proof, alongside experiments across several sparse training methods. Those experiments show accuracy improvements when S²-SAM is added to the tested methods. The contribution is therefore both an explanation of why sparse optimization can be difficult and a broadly applicable optimization modification supported by theoretical analysis and empirical results.
neurips-2024-a-single-step-sharpness-awa.tldr: S²-SAM reuses prior gradients to improve sparse training with a single-step sharpness-aware update that the authors report adds no extra cost.

paragraphs: To synthesize convincing audio at a listener’s location, a system needs to describe how sound travels through a scene before arriving there. An impulse response captures these propagation effects over time. This paper introduces Acoustic Volume Rendering, or AVR, to learn a field of impulse responses that can produce responses for previously unseen poses.

AVR adapts volume rendering, a technique used for image and scene representations, to the acoustic setting. Because impulse responses are time-series signals, the authors develop rendering in the frequency domain and use spherical integration to fit measured responses. The resulting representation incorporates wave propagation principles into how the acoustic field is modeled.

Experiments report state-of-the-art synthesis of impulse responses at novel poses, with a substantial improvement over the compared leading methods. The authors also introduce AcoustiX, an acoustic simulation platform reported to produce more accurate and realistic responses than existing simulators. Together, the contributions address both learning spatially varying acoustics and generating the simulated acoustic measurements used to study them.
neurips-2024-acoustic-volume-rendering-f.tldr: AVR adapts volume rendering to acoustic signals, learning impulse response fields that improve sound propagation synthesis at unseen poses.

paragraphs: Cooperation becomes difficult when what benefits an individual agent differs from what benefits the group. Existing approaches often encourage cooperation through manually designed rewards or extra mechanisms. This paper instead examines how the learning updates themselves can gradually bring individual and collective objectives into alignment.

The authors represent mixed-motive interaction as a differentiable game, making its learning dynamics accessible to gradient-based analysis. Their method, Altruistic Gradient Adjustment, or AgA, modifies gradients to promote alignment while still considering individual interests. The theoretical result concerns attraction toward stable fixed points of the collective objective, giving the adjustment a mathematical foundation beyond manual reward design.

The paper supplies empirical support using the two-player public good game, the sequential social dilemma environments Cleanup and Harvest, and a larger environment developed in StarCraft II. These settings examine cooperation at different scales. The findings support gradient adjustment as a way to encourage collective behavior; the stated theoretical target is stable collective fixed points, rather than a claim that every interaction reaches a globally best cooperative outcome.
neurips-2024-aligning-individual-and-col.tldr: AgA adjusts learning gradients to align individual and collective objectives, with theoretical and empirical support for more cooperative dynamics.

paragraphs: Learning a causal graph requires choosing interventions that reveal how variables influence one another. This paper introduces CAASL, a policy that selects interventions adaptively and in real time without requiring access to a likelihood. Its aim is to learn the intervention-selection strategy in advance so that it can be reused during new causal investigations.

CAASL uses a transformer network trained through reinforcement learning in a simulator of the experimental environment. Its reward measures how closely the causal-graph posterior inferred from collected data matches the true graph. This connects intervention choice directly to the quality of causal inference, rather than treating data collection as a separate preliminary step.

On synthetic data and a single-cell gene expression simulator, data collected by CAASL produces better graph estimates than the alternative strategies tested. The policy also generalizes empirically to shifted test environments. Reported zero-shot results include environments with more variables than those used in training and unfamiliar intervention types, suggesting that the learned strategy can transfer beyond its original training configuration.
neurips-2024-amortized-active-causal-ind.tldr: CAASL learns a reusable intervention-selection policy that improves causal graph estimation and transfers to several unfamiliar experimental settings.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts large pretrained models with little computational overhead. The authors identify a problem with this adaptation: models can remain accurate while becoming severely underconfident, especially when only a few examples are available. They also lack sufficiently precise uncertainty estimates, so prediction quality alone does not capture how reliably they communicate what they know.

Bayesian-PEFT adds two lightweight Bayesian components to existing fine-tuning techniques. A base rate adjustment strengthens prior belief associated with knowledge learned during pretraining, increasing confidence. An evidential ensemble then combines multiple components, using belief regularization to encourage diversity among them. These mechanisms address both confidence in retained knowledge and the quality of uncertainty estimates.

The paper provides theoretical analysis supporting accurate, reliable adaptation with calibrated uncertainty. Experiments span different datasets, few-shot settings, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, reporting strong prediction and calibration performance. The significance is that adaptation is evaluated on two connected requirements: making correct predictions and assigning confidence that appropriately reflects their reliability.
neurips-2024-be-confident-in-what-you-kn.tldr: Bayesian-PEFT combines prior adjustment and a diverse evidential ensemble to improve confidence calibration and prediction during few-shot adaptation.

paragraphs: A useful embodied assistant needs to understand both what a person wants to accomplish and what that person can physically do. CHAIC turns this requirement into a cooperation challenge. An agent observes from its own viewpoint and helps a human complete household or outdoor tasks, including situations involving limited reach or wheelchair use.

Success requires two linked capabilities. The helper must infer intentions and physical constraints by following the person and observing behavior. It must then build a cooperative plan tailored to that partner, with the goal of completing the task quickly together. This makes assistance depend on understanding the particular human rather than simply executing a task independently.

The benchmark introduces four agents with physical constraints and eight long-horizon tasks across indoor and outdoor settings, including emergencies and potential risks. The authors evaluate planning-based and learning-based baselines and introduce a method combining large language models with behavior modeling. Their empirical findings support CHAIC as a systematic way to assess social perception and cooperative planning in embodied agents.
neurips-2024-constrained-human-ai-cooper.tldr: CHAIC evaluates whether embodied assistants can infer a human partner’s intentions and physical constraints and adapt their cooperative plans accordingly.

paragraphs: Pretrained diffusion models generate images, but the desired output may instead be a parameterized representation, such as a panorama or a 3D NeRF. This paper introduces a training-free method for sampling these differentiable representations. Its central objective is to obtain varied samples, going beyond procedures that mainly search for a particularly favored output.

The method transfers the reverse-time diffusion dynamics from image space into the representation’s parameter space. The authors describe this as pulling back the process: the representation’s parameters are updated according to the transferred dynamics. They also identify an implicit constraint that the representation places on possible samples and show that accounting for it improves consistency and detail.

Experiments cover images, panoramas, and 3D NeRFs, reporting substantial improvements in both quality and diversity over existing techniques. These findings matter because quality alone would not establish that a procedure samples a useful range of outputs. The work presents a general-purpose route for applying pretrained diffusion models to representations whose parameters, rather than image pixels alone, must be generated.
neurips-2024-diffusing-differentiable-re.tldr: A training-free method transfers diffusion dynamics into representation parameters, improving the quality and diversity of images, panoramas, and 3D NeRFs.

paragraphs: Deep neural networks perform strongly on images, video, and text, yet tabular data remains a setting where gradient boosting decision trees often have an advantage. This paper addresses that gap through architecture design. It introduces DOFEN, a neural network inspired by oblivious decision trees and organized as a deep forest ensemble.

The central property highlighted by the authors is on-off sparse selection of columns. For tabular inputs, columns represent the information available to the model, so selecting them is a direct way to control which inputs participate in its computation. DOFEN brings this tree-inspired selection behavior into a neural architecture, connecting a strength of tabular modeling with deep learning.

The authors evaluate DOFEN on Tabular Benchmark, which contains 73 datasets across many domains. They report that it surpasses other neural networks and achieves state-of-the-art performance on that benchmark. The clearly stated comparison establishes a strong neural approach to tabular prediction; the motivation involving gradient boosting should be kept distinct from the explicit finding about outperforming other neural networks.
neurips-2024-dofen-deep-oblivious-forest.tldr: DOFEN uses tree-inspired sparse column selection to achieve leading neural-network performance on a benchmark of 73 tabular datasets.

paragraphs: An overall benchmark score can leave unclear how a language model performs as problems become harder. Many existing datasets lack reliable, continuous difficulty labels for individual questions. Easy2Hard addresses this measurement gap with six benchmark datasets covering domains that include mathematics, programming, chess puzzles, and reasoning.

The authors estimate difficulty using performance records from many people and language models on established leaderboards. They apply recognized ranking approaches, including Item Response Theory and Glicko-2, to assign standardized problem scores. Difficulty is therefore grounded in observed performance, giving researchers a basis for examining model behavior across a range of challenge levels.

The collection includes a substantially greater proportion of difficult problems than previous collections, making it a demanding evaluation resource. Experiments with six state-of-the-art language models examine performance and generalization across the difficulty range. The contribution is a way to profile where models succeed and struggle more precisely, rather than treating all questions in a dataset as equally informative about their capabilities.
neurips-2024-easy2hard-bench-standardize.tldr: Easy2Hard provides six datasets with performance-derived difficulty scores for evaluating how language-model capabilities change as problems become harder.

paragraphs: Generalized eigenvalue problems underlie statistical methods including principal component analysis, Fisher’s discriminant analysis, and canonical correlation analysis. This paper studies what happens when the leading generalized eigenvector is assumed to come from a generative model. That assumption restricts the search to vectors that the generator can produce.

The generator is required to be Lipschitz continuous, meaning its outputs change in a controlled way as its inputs change. Under appropriate additional conditions, the authors show that any optimal solution of their formulation achieves the optimal statistical rate. This result concerns the quality of estimation when the assumed generative structure and the theorem’s conditions hold.

To address computation, the paper proposes the Projected Rayleigh Flow Method, an iterative algorithm for approximating that solution. Under suitable assumptions, it converges linearly to an estimated vector that also achieves the optimal statistical rate. Numerical results demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The work thus connects a structured assumption about the target vector to both statistical guarantees and a practical iterative procedure.
neurips-2024-generalized-eigenvalue-prob.tldr: Generative priors enable statistically optimal generalized eigenvector estimation and a linearly convergent algorithm under suitable assumptions.

paragraphs: Sharpness-aware minimization, or SAM, is known to improve generalization, but this paper studies its behavior through a different quantity: balancedness. For scale-invariant problems involving two groups of variables, balancedness is defined using the difference between their squared norms. This viewpoint is motivated by architectures such as LoRA and exposes behavior beyond the usual focus on loss sharpness.

The theoretical and empirical analysis finds that SAM encourages the two variable groups to become balanced. It also finds that this effect responds to the data, with outliers exerting a stronger influence. That observation is consistent with empirical results showing SAM outperforming stochastic gradient descent in the presence of outliers.

The authors use this insight to develop balancedness-aware regularization, or BAR, for scale-invariant problems, including language-model fine-tuning with LoRA. Across tasks involving RoBERTa, GPT2, and OPT-1.3B, BAR saves 95% of SAM’s computational overhead while improving test performance. This percentage concerns the extra overhead associated with SAM, rather than a claim of reducing total training computation by 95%.
neurips-2024-implicit-regularization-of-.tldr: Analyzing SAM’s tendency to balance parameter groups leads to BAR, which saves 95% of SAM’s overhead in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Programming by examples asks a system to infer an algorithm from a small set of input-output pairs. Strong code generation does not by itself establish that a model can infer the intended rule from examples. This paper tests that capability directly, examining whether large language models have effectively solved this form of inductive programming.

The experiments include familiar list and string tasks and a less common graphics programming domain that is poorly represented in typical pretraining data. The authors find that pretrained models are ineffective at these programming-by-example tasks. Fine-tuning produces much stronger performance, provided the test problems come from the same distribution as the training problems.

The study also analyzes empirical causes of success and failure and investigates steps toward better generalization outside the training distribution. Its conclusion is qualified: language models make substantial progress on the usual task suite and could broaden the flexibility of programming-by-example systems. The dependence on in-distribution testing remains central to interpreting that progress, so these results do not establish that the overall problem is solved.
neurips-2024-is-programming-by-example-s.tldr: Fine-tuning substantially improves programming by examples on in-distribution tasks, but pretrained performance and broader generalization still fall short.

paragraphs: Some learning problems treat each collection of observations as samples from a probability distribution. The object to compare or predict from is then a distribution, rather than a single observation. Kernel methods provide a way to compare such objects, but choosing an appropriate distribution kernel can be difficult, particularly for regression.

This paper proposes learning a data-dependent distribution kernel without supervision. Its objective maximizes entropy in the space of probability-measure embeddings, where distributions are represented for comparison. This turns kernel selection into a learning problem guided by the arrangement of distribution representations, rather than requiring a suitable kernel to be chosen beforehand.

The authors analyze the latent space produced by this objective and show that its geometry is well suited to downstream discriminative tasks. They also demonstrate the learned kernel’s performance across different modalities. The contribution links an unsupervised representation-learning principle to the needs of later prediction tasks, providing both theoretical motivation for the resulting geometry and empirical evidence of usefulness.
neurips-2024-learning-to-embed-distribut.tldr: An entropy-maximization objective learns distribution kernels without supervision, producing embedding geometry suited to downstream discrimination.

paragraphs: In heterogeneous graphs, different node and relation types make distant connections potentially informative but difficult to use efficiently. Simply incorporating more remote information also risks over-smoothing, which reduces distinctions between node representations. This paper studies how to select useful long-range meta-paths: typed routes through the graph that connect information to a target node type.

The proposed LMSPS framework begins with a search space containing all meta-paths associated with the target type. A progressive sampling algorithm gradually narrows that space, with the stated search-time complexity independent of hop count. A sampling-based evaluation then identifies effective paths, and the model is retrained using only those selected paths.

This selection is intended to reduce both computational cost and over-smoothing by focusing on useful long-range information. Experiments across diverse heterogeneous graph datasets show that LMSPS discovers effective distant paths and outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support searching for the right typed connections as a way to benefit from graph distance without indiscriminately incorporating every available route.
neurips-2024-long-range-meta-path-search.tldr: LMSPS progressively searches for useful long-range meta-paths, improving heterogeneous graph learning while mitigating computation and over-smoothing.

paragraphs: An adversarial attack on a multiclass classifier must decide which incorrect class to target. The authors argue that choosing targets mainly from classifier confidence is a naive strategy. MALT, short for Mesoscopic Almost Linearity Targeting, replaces that choice with a method based on assumptions that the model behaves approximately linearly in a local region.

The idea is to use that local structure to guide target selection. Although the method draws inspiration from linear predictors, the paper provides a formal argument and empirical evidence that it also applies to nonlinear models. The relevant assumption is approximate local linearity, so the approach does not require the entire classifier to be linear.

On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet with different robust models, the resulting attack matches AutoAttack’s successful attacks and reaches additional samples that AutoAttack did not attack successfully. The authors report an attack strategy five times faster than AutoAttack’s. These results indicate that target selection can materially affect both attack effectiveness and efficiency, and therefore the strength of the robustness assessment obtained.
neurips-2024-malt-powers-up-adversarial-.tldr: MALT uses local approximate linearity to select attack targets, surpassing AutoAttack’s coverage with a reported five-times-faster strategy.

paragraphs: Meta-DT addresses the challenge of training reinforcement-learning agents from existing experience so they can generalize to unseen tasks. It combines transformer sequence modeling with a learned task representation. A pretrained, context-aware world model extracts a compact description of the task, which then conditions a causal transformer’s task-oriented sequence generation.

The framework also uses trajectories generated by its own meta-policy as prompts. It selects the trajectory segment where the pretrained world model makes the largest prediction error. The aim is to supply task-specific information that complements what the world model already captures, making the agent’s own history an additional source of guidance.

At test time, Meta-DT does not require expert demonstrations or domain knowledge. Experiments on MuJoCo and Meta-World, across multiple dataset types, report better few-shot and zero-shot generalization than strong baselines. The findings support combining a compact learned task description with carefully selected experience, while the absence of those test-time prerequisites makes the framework more practical within the evaluated offline meta-learning setting.
neurips-2024-meta-dt-offline-meta-rl-as-.tldr: Meta-DT combines world-model task representations with self-generated trajectory prompts to improve offline agents’ generalization to unseen tasks.

paragraphs: Vision-language models sometimes describe objects that are absent from an image. This paper investigates how that problem changes when a model must attend to several objects simultaneously. It shifts evaluation beyond checking whether a single object class is present toward examining individual entities and the distractions that arise in multi-object scenes.

The authors introduce ROPE, an automated evaluation protocol that accounts for the distribution of object classes within each image. It uses visual referring prompts to clarify which objects are being discussed. These choices help examine multi-object recognition while reducing ambiguity about the intended visual targets.

The experiments find more hallucination when models focus on multiple objects than when they focus on one. Hallucination also changes with the tested class distribution, suggesting possible reliance on shortcuts and spurious correlations. Other influences include salience, frequency, data-specific factors, and intrinsic model behavior. The contribution is an evaluation framework and empirical account of these effects, giving researchers a way to measure progress toward more reliable reasoning about realistic scenes.
neurips-2024-multi-object-hallucination-.tldr: ROPE reveals that tested vision-language models hallucinate more when attending to multiple objects, with behavior affected by object distributions and other factors.

paragraphs: Gradient-based training often requires careful selection of update sizes and other hyperparameters. Clipped gradient descent adds a clipping threshold to control excessively large gradients, increasing the tuning burden. This paper examines how to remove that burden for clipped optimization, extending attention beyond earlier parameter-free work focused on step sizes alone.

The authors propose Inexact Polyak Stepsize, a method with convergence to the optimum without hyperparameter tuning under the stated assumptions. They analyze both L-smooth losses and losses satisfying the specified (L₀, L₁)-smoothness condition. Its convergence rate is asymptotically independent of L, matching that particular property of clipped gradient descent with well-tuned hyperparameters.

The theoretical convergence results are checked numerically using a synthetic function, and practical effectiveness is demonstrated with LSTM, Nano-GPT, and T5. The contribution connects automatic adjustment with guarantees usually associated with carefully configured optimization. The smoothness assumptions remain part of the theoretical claim, while the model experiments provide separate empirical evidence that the proposed methods can be useful in training.
neurips-2024-parameter-free-clipped-grad.tldr: Inexact Polyak Stepsize removes hyperparameter tuning from clipped gradient optimization, with conditional convergence guarantees and neural-model experiments.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders offer a framework for interpreting sensory inputs through Bayesian inference, but their usual continuous latent variables differ from discrete neural activity. This paper introduces the Poisson VAE, which represents inputs using discrete spike counts. The architecture combines Poisson-distributed latent variables with principles of predictive coding to study brain-like sensory representation.

That combination introduces a metabolic cost term into the model’s loss. The authors identify a connection between this cost and sparse coding and verify the relationship empirically. This gives the architecture an interpretable link between how it represents information and a cost associated with the activity used to encode it.

The paper also compares the geometry of its learned representations with alternative VAEs. The Poisson VAE uses relatively higher-dimensional representations, which facilitate separating categories with a linear classifier in the downstream task. The reported classification result has fivefold better sample efficiency. Together, these findings provide a computational framework for examining sensory inference while connecting the discrete representation to measurable properties of learned features.
neurips-2024-poisson-variational-autoenc.tldr: The Poisson VAE encodes inputs as spike counts, linking predictive coding to sparsity and reporting fivefold better downstream classification sample efficiency.

paragraphs: When an image contains people, an application may need the pose and outline of one particular person. This paper introduces Referring Human Pose and Mask Estimation, where text or a positional prompt identifies that person. The task combines identity-aware selection with prediction of both body keypoints and a segmentation mask.

The authors create RefHuman by extending MS COCO with text and positional prompt annotations. It contains more than 50,000 annotated instances, each pairing prompts with keypoints and masks. This provides training and evaluation data for a task in which selecting the correct individual is part of the prediction problem itself.

Their end-to-end method, UniPHD, extracts multimodal representations and uses a pose-centric hierarchical decoder to process person-level and keypoint queries. Its outputs correspond to the person specified by the prompt. Experiments report high-quality prompted results and top-tier performance on RefHuman validation and MS COCO val2017. The combined representation has potential uses in assistive robotics and sports analysis, where both a person’s posture and occupied image region matter.
neurips-2024-referring-human-pose-and-ma.tldr: RefHuman and UniPHD enable text- or position-guided prediction of the pose and segmentation mask of a specified person.

paragraphs: Edge-cloud collaborative inference lets resource-limited devices share deep-learning computation with a cloud server while keeping raw inputs on the device. However, information sent during that computation can still expose the input or the model’s prediction. This paper treats those two forms of leakage as targets for a defense called InfoScissors.

InfoScissors aims to reduce mutual information between intermediate model outputs and both the device’s inputs and predictions. In plain language, it tries to make the shared intermediate results reveal less about those protected quantities. The objective therefore addresses leakage through the representation exchanged during inference, beyond simply withholding the original data.

The authors evaluate the defense on several datasets under diverse attacks and report superiority over the compared approaches. They also theoretically analyze weaknesses in recent mutual-information defenses, particularly those based on the Variational Information Bottleneck, and provide analysis of their own method. The work connects a practical privacy objective to a critique of how information-based defenses are formulated, supported by both attack evaluations and theory.
neurips-2024-reimagining-mutual-informat.tldr: InfoScissors reduces information leakage from shared intermediate representations, targeting exposure of both device inputs and predictions.

paragraphs: Learning safety constraints through trial and error is problematic for real-world reinforcement learning. Expert demonstrations can convey safety preferences, but imitating an entire policy makes new tasks depend on additional demonstrations. This paper focuses on learning the safety aspects from expert data while leaving task-specific behavior available to reinforcement learning.

This goal belongs to inverse constrained reinforcement learning, which infers constraints from observed behavior. Earlier approaches used complex optimization involving three levels. The authors argue that this difficult optimization structure contributes to weaker performance on benchmark tasks, and introduce a simplified constraint-inference framework motivated by inverse reinforcement learning.

Across continuous-control benchmarks, the simplified framework performs as well as or better than prior work. The authors also report that it is easier to implement and tune and more readily supports extensions such as offline constraint inference. The practical significance is a more manageable way to extract reusable safety information, especially when expert behavior is imperfect or imprecise, without requiring imitation to supply the whole task policy.
neurips-2024-simplifying-constraint-infe.tldr: A simplified constraint-inference framework learns safety aspects from demonstrations while matching or improving prior continuous-control benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression searches for compact programs or mathematical expressions that explain a dataset. Genetic algorithms are a common way to explore possible hypotheses. This paper introduces LaSR, which augments that search with a library of abstract concepts expressed in text and discovered through a large language model.

LaSR asks the language model, through zero-shot queries, to identify and evolve concepts found in already successful hypotheses. It then generates new candidates using a mixture of ordinary evolutionary operations and language-model-guided steps conditioned on those concepts. Successful new hypotheses feed back into another round of concept abstraction, so the library and the search develop together.

On the Feynman equations benchmark and synthetic tasks, LaSR substantially outperforms several state-of-the-art symbolic regression approaches based on deep learning and evolutionary algorithms. The authors also demonstrate discovery of a new scaling law for language models. The contribution is a feedback loop that turns patterns in promising expressions into reusable guidance for further search, rather than treating each candidate only as an isolated program.
neurips-2024-symbolic-regression-with-a-.tldr: LaSR improves symbolic regression by using an LLM to build and evolve a concept library that guides evolutionary search.

paragraphs: Atmospheric turbulence distorts long-range video through fluctuations in how the atmosphere refracts light. Restoring individual frames does not necessarily produce a coherent video, because the distortions vary across space and time. This paper introduces ConVRT to improve consistency across frames while mitigating those turbulence effects.

ConVRT builds on the observation that turbulence introduces high-frequency temporal variation. Its neural video representation separates spatial content from temporal deformation, allowing the temporal part to be regularized specifically. The regularized representation acts as a low-pass filter, suppressing the rapid temporal variations associated with turbulence and promoting more stable restored sequences.

The training framework combines supervised pretraining on synthetic turbulence with self-supervised learning on real-world videos. This links learning from controlled synthetic examples to restoration of actual recordings. The authors report significantly improved temporal consistency across diverse real-world data. The key contribution is the connection between a physical observation about turbulence and a representation whose temporal behavior can be directly controlled, making coherence across frames an explicit part of restoration.
neurips-2024-temporally-consistent-atmos.tldr: ConVRT separates video content from temporal deformation to suppress turbulence-related variation and improve consistency across restored frames.

paragraphs: GAN architectures often accumulate empirical tricks intended to stabilize training and preserve output variety. This paper investigates whether a more principled training objective can replace those additions. The authors derive a regularized relativistic GAN loss designed to address mode dropping and non-convergence, two issues that have motivated complicated training recipes.

Their mathematical analysis establishes local convergence guarantees for the proposed loss, unlike most existing relativistic losses. Local convergence is the scope of that guarantee. With the new objective in place, the authors simplify and modernize the architecture, using StyleGAN2 as a starting example and replacing older backbones with modern components to produce R3GAN.

Experiments report that this minimalist baseline outperforms StyleGAN2 on FFHQ, ImageNet, CIFAR, and Stacked MNIST. It also compares favorably with state-of-the-art GANs and diffusion models. The findings provide evidence that strong GAN performance need not depend on an accumulation of ad hoc techniques: a better-founded loss can support both architectural simplification and competitive generation in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-the-gan-is-dead-long-live-t.tldr: R3GAN combines a regularized loss with local convergence guarantees and modern architecture to deliver a simpler, competitive GAN baseline.
